Let’s restate the dependencies in simpler form:

1.  Given facts (definitely true):
    s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue.

2.  From those, “wide” is true because s0∧s1∧s2∧s3 is true.

3.  q is derived by the rule  
       t0 ∧ wide ∧ etrue ⇒ q.  
    Since wide and etrue are already true, q will be true exactly if t0 is true.

4.  The t‐chain is  
       qcore ⇒ t5 ⇒ t4 ⇒ t3 ⇒ t2 ⇒ t1 ⇒ t0.  
    (Each “⇒” is the given “is true if” rule.)

5.  qcore itself is true if either x0a or x1a is true (two separate rules).  
    But x0a and x0b are complements (one must be true, but we don’t know which), and x1a and x1b are complements (again one is true, but unknown which).

Thus whether qcore holds depends on unknown choices for x0a and x1a.  
– If x0a or x1a is true → qcore → the whole t‐chain fires → t0 → q is true.  
– If both x0a and x1a are false → qcore fails → t‐chain fails → t0 is not derived → q is false.

Since we have no further information about x0a or x1a, we cannot decide whether qcore (and hence q) holds.  

ANSWER: C

Let us work bottom‐up following Prolog’s negation‐as‐failure (NAF) and operational semantics:

1. Facts and easy goals  
   – s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue are all true by fact.  
   – wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3 succeeds.  
   – t0 ← t1, and q ← t0, wide, etrue, so q reduces to proving t1.

2. The t‐chain  
   t1←t2←t3←t4←t5←qcore  
   so t1 (hence t0) succeeds exactly if qcore succeeds.

3. The definition of qcore  
   qcore ← x0a.  
   qcore ← x1a.

4. The x0a/x0b and x1a/x1b mutual loops  
   x0a ← not x0b  
   x0b ← not x0a  
   x1a ← not x1b  
   x1b ← not x1a  

   Each of these four goals sits in an even cycle through negation.  
   – Attempting x0a: Prolog tries to prove not x0b, so it calls x0b.  
     x0b tries not x0a, which re-invokes x0a, …  
   – No branch finitely succeeds or finitely fails; instead it loops/flounders.  
   – Likewise for x1a/x1b.

5. Consequences for qcore and q  
   – The first clause qcore ← x0a does not finitely succeed or fail (it loops).  
     Hence Prolog does not “fail” that clause and move on.  
   – Nor does it give a definite failure on x0a that would allow backtracking to x1a.  
   – So qcore itself neither succeeds nor finitely fails—it is stuck.  
   – Therefore t5, t4, …, t1, t0, and ultimately q all get stuck.

Conclusion: under Prolog’s NAF (closed‐world) operational reading no proof of q ever terminates with success or finite failure. Hence:

ANSWER: C

Let’s restate the program more compactly:

  Facts:
    s0.  s1.  s2.  s3.  etrue.
    wide :- s0, s1, s2, s3.     (so wide is a fact)
  
  Choice‐pairs (odd negation‐loops):
    x0a :- not x0b.
    x0b :- not x0a.
    x1a :- not x1b.
    x1b :- not x1a.
  
  qcore :- x0a.
  qcore :- x1a.
  
  t5 :- qcore.
  t4 :- t5.
  t3 :- t4.
  t2 :- t3.
  t1 :- t2.
  t0 :- t1.
  
  q :- t0, wide, etrue.

We observe:

1. wide is true (all s0–s3 are facts) and etrue is a fact.
2. To get q we need t0, which depends through t1…t5 on qcore.
3. qcore is true in any answer set where at least one of x0a or x1a is chosen.
4. The two independent choice‐loops {x0a,x0b} and {x1a,x1b} yield 4 total answer sets.  In 3 of them x0a or x1a (or both) is true, hence qcore holds, hence t5…t0 and finally q hold.
5. Thus there are answer sets with q true (and one without), so q is true in at least one answer set.

Under credulous (brave) reasoning that means “Definitely yes.”

ANSWER: A

Let’s enumerate the mutually independent “switches” and see in which answer‐sets q holds:

1. Facts (in every answer set):  
   s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue ⇒ wide is derived (since wide ← s0,s1,s2,s3).

2. Two independent default‐negation loops:  
   (a) x0b ← not x0a  
       x0a ← not x0b  
       ⇒ exactly one of {x0a, x0b} in each answer set.  
   (b) x1a ← not x1b  
       x1b ← not x1a  
       ⇒ exactly one of {x1a, x1b} in each answer set.  

   These two loops together yield 4 combinations of {x0a/x0b}×{x1a/x1b}.

3. qcore ← x0a.  
   qcore ← x1a.  
   ⇒ qcore is true iff at least one of x0a,x1a is true.

4. The t-chain:  
   t5 ← qcore; then by positive rules t4←t5←…←t1←t2←t3←t4  
   and t0 ← t1.  
   So if qcore is true then t0 is true; if qcore is false then all ti (including t0) stay false.

5. Finally q ← t0,wide,etrue.  Since wide and etrue are always true, q holds exactly when t0 is true, i.e. exactly when qcore is true.

Now check the four cases:

  1. x0a= T, x1a= T ⇒ qcore= T ⇒ t0= T ⇒ q= T  
  2. x0a= T, x1a= F ⇒ qcore= T ⇒ t0= T ⇒ q= T  
  3. x0a= F, x1a= T ⇒ qcore= T ⇒ t0= T ⇒ q= T  
  4. x0a= F, x1a= F ⇒ qcore= F ⇒ t0= F ⇒ q= F

In the fourth answer set q is false. Hence q is not true in every answer set. ANSWER: B

Let’s identify all facts and rules, then compute the well‐founded model step by step.

Facts (definitely true):  
  s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue.  

From these,  
  wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3  
whence wide is definitely true.

Next we have two “odd” negation‐cycles:  
  x0a ← not x0b  
  x0b ← not x0a  
and  
  x1a ← not x1b  
  x1b ← not x1a  

Under the well‐founded semantics each of x0a, x0b, x1a, x1b is assigned undefined (no grounded support, no rule body is definitely true).

Now  
  qcore ← x0a  
  qcore ← x1a  
both bodies are undefined, so qcore has no founded proof (but also isn’t refuted)—it remains undefined in the well‐founded model.

The t‐chain is  
  t1 ← t2  
  t2 ← t3  
  t3 ← t4  
  t4 ← t5  
  t5 ← qcore  
  t0 ← t1  

Since qcore is undefined, none of t5, t4, t3, t2, t1, t0 can become true, and they participate in a positive loop dependent on undefined qcore. Hence all t0…t5 are undefined.

Finally  
  q ← t0, wide, etrue.  
wide and etrue are true, but t0 is undefined, so the body of the unique rule for q is undefined. q therefore is undefined in the well‐founded model.

Undefined means “neither definitely true nor definitely false,” so the correct answer is:

ANSWER: C

Let’s restate the rules more schematically and then look for possible truth‐value assignments:

1.  q  is true ⇐ qcore ∧ etrue  
2.  x1b is true ⇐ ¬x1a  
3.  x1a is true ⇐ ¬x1b  
4.  x0a is true ⇐ ¬x0b  
5.  etrue is true  
6.  qcore is true ⇐ x0a  
7.  qcore is true ⇐ x1a  
8.  x0b is true ⇐ ¬x0a  

Since etrue is given true, q is equivalent to qcore.  And qcore is true exactly if x0a or x1a is true.  

But x1a and x1b form a “negation‐cycle”:
   – If x1a is false, rule 2 forces x1b true  
   – If x1b is false, rule 3 forces x1a true  
Hence exactly one of x1a,x1b must be true—but we cannot tell which.  
Similarly x0a,x0b form the same pattern, so exactly one of x0a,x0b is true, but we don’t know which.

Thus there are two (or more) models:
– Model 1: x1a=true, x1b=false, x0a=false, x0b=true ⇒ qcore is true (via x1a) ⇒ q=true.  
– Model 2: x1a=false, x1b=true, x0a=false, x0b=true ⇒ qcore is false ⇒ q=false.  

Because both outcomes are consistent with the rules, q is not determined uniquely.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s restate the rules in Prolog‐style form (negation = “not …”):

1. q      :- qcore, etrue.
2. qcore  :- x0a.
3. qcore  :- x1a.
4. x0a    :- not x0b.
5. x0b    :- not x0a.
6. x1a    :- not x1b.
7. x1b    :- not x1a.
8. etrue.   % a fact

We ask: does q finitely succeed (⇒ “Definitely yes”), finitely fail (⇒ “Definitely no”), or neither (⇒ “Cannot be determined”)?

Step 1: etrue is a fact, so it succeeds immediately.

Step 2: To prove q we must prove qcore first.

Step 3: qcore has two clauses, so Prolog will try them in order:

  A) qcore :- x0a.
     To prove x0a, Prolog invokes not x0b.
     But to evaluate not x0b, it attempts x0b:
       x0b :- not x0a.
       To evaluate that, it needs not x0a ⇒ it tries x0a … we’re back where we started.
     Hence the subproof for x0a (and so for qcore via x0a) never terminates—there is an infinite loop due to the mutual negation of x0a and x0b.

  B) On backtracking, Prolog tries the second clause:
     qcore :- x1a.
     To prove x1a, it invokes not x1b.
     But x1b depends on not x1a, which in turn depends on x1a … again an infinite loop (mutual negation between x1a and x1b).

Since both alternatives for qcore lead to non-terminating negation loops, Prolog never gets a definite success or finite failure. Consequently, qcore “cannot be determined,” and hence q itself cannot be determined (the call for q never terminates, it flounders).

Therefore, under closed‐world negation‐as‐failure with Prolog operational semantics, the correct answer is:

ANSWER: C

Let’s identify the informal mutual‐exclusion “choice” pairs and then see where q ends up true.

1. etrue is a fact, so etrue holds in every answer set.  
2. x1a ∶− not x1b and x1b ∶− not x1a form an exclusive choice: each answer set has exactly one of {x1a, x1b}.  
3. x0a ∶− not x0b and x0b ∶− not x0a likewise force exactly one of {x0a, x0b}.  
4. qcore ∶− x0a.  
   qcore ∶− x1a.  
5. q ∶− qcore, etrue.  

Thus there are 2×2=4 candidate models, based on (x1a or x1b) × (x0a or x0b).  In three of these four (whenever x1a or x0a is chosen) we get qcore and hence q (since etrue is always present).  Only in the single case {x1b, x0b} do we fail to derive q.  Therefore q is true in at least one answer set.

ANSWER: A

Let’s identify the default‐negation cycles and their effect:

1. Facts and simple rules  
   – etrue is unconditionally true.  
   – q ← qcore, etrue.

2. Two independent mutual‐default pairs:  
   a) x1a ← not x1b.  
      x1b ← not x1a.  
   b) x0a ← not x0b.  
      x0b ← not x0a.

   Each pair has two stable choices: one atom true, the other false.

3. qcore is derived if either x0a or x1a holds:
   – qcore ← x0a.  
   – qcore ← x1a.

4. Thus across both pairs there are 2×2=4 candidate answer sets:

   Case 1: x1a, x0a  
     → qcore by x0a or x1a → q (since etrue).  
   Case 2: x1b, x0a  
     → qcore by x0a → q.  
   Case 3: x1a, x0b  
     → qcore by x1a → q.  
   Case 4: x1b, x0b  
     → neither x0a nor x1a holds → qcore fails → q fails.

5. In three models q is true, but in the fourth (x1b,x0b) q is false.

Since there is at least one answer set where q does not hold, under skeptical (cautious) reasoning q is not guaranteed.

ANSWER: B

Let us identify the strongly connected components (SCCs) and see how the well-founded semantics assigns truth values:

1. etrue is a fact, so etrue = true.

2. The pair of rules
     x1a :- not x1b.
     x1b :- not x1a.
   is an even negation cycle with two stable models ({x1a} and {x1b}) but no grounded support.  Under well-founded semantics both x1a and x1b are assigned undefined.

3. Similarly
     x0a :- not x0b.
     x0b :- not x0a.
   is the same pattern.  Thus x0a = undefined and x0b = undefined.

4. qcore has two rules
     qcore :- x0a.
     qcore :- x1a.
   Both bodies are based on atoms (x0a, x1a) that are undefined.  No rule fires to make qcore true, nor is there any grounded reason to mark qcore false.  So qcore = undefined.

5. Finally
     q :- qcore, etrue.
   Since etrue = true but qcore = undefined, this rule cannot establish q as true.  Nor is there any other rule to support q, so q likewise remains undefined in the well-founded model.

Because q is neither founded true nor founded false, its status in well-founded semantics is undefined.

ANSWER: C

Let’s restate the rules more symbolically (all implications are one–way “if … then”):

1. x1a ⇒ qcore  
2. ¬x0a ⇒ x0b  
3. ¬x1a ⇒ x1b  
4. ¬x0b ⇒ x0a  
5. x0a ⇒ qcore  
6. qcore ⇒ q  
7. ¬x1b ⇒ x1a  

From (2) and (4) we get x0b ↔ ¬x0a, and from (3) and (7) we get x1b ↔ ¬x1a.  Thus exactly one of x0a,x0b is true, and exactly one of x1a,x1b is true.

Case 1: x0a = true.  
Then by (5) qcore is true, so by (6) q is true.

Case 2: x0a = false (hence x0b=true).  
  – If x1a = true then by (1) qcore=true ⇒ q=true.  
  – If x1a = false then x1b=true, so neither (1) nor (5) fires and qcore can be false, whence q can be false.

Since we can find consistent assignments making q true and others making q false, q is not determined.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s try to prove q by a Prolog‐style search under negation‐as‐failure:

1. To prove q, we need to prove qcore.  
2. The clauses for qcore are tried in order:  
   (a) qcore :- x1a.  
   (b) qcore :- x0a.  

3. First we attempt x1a:  
   • x1a :- not x1b.  
   • To check not x1b, we must see if x1b finitely fails.  
   • x1b :- not x1a.  
   • To check not x1a, we must see if x1a finitely fails. But x1a is our original goal!  
   • This leads to an infinite alternation:
       x1a → not x1b → x1b → not x1a → x1a → …  
     which never terminates or finitely fails.

   Because the first clause for qcore (via x1a) loops indefinitely, it does not yield either a success or a finite failure; Prolog does not backtrack to try the second clause.

4. Since the first branch neither succeeds nor finitely fails, the overall proof for q cannot terminate with “true” or “false.”

By the given operational rule (“If evaluating the goal does not terminate or gets stuck because of negation … answer ‘Cannot be determined.’”), we must conclude:

ANSWER: C

Let us name the rules more succinctly:

 1. qcore ← x1a.  
 2. x0b   ← not x0a.  
 3. x1b   ← not x1a.  
 4. x0a   ← not x0b.  
 5. qcore ← x0a.  
 6. q     ← qcore.  
 7. x1a   ← not x1b.  

We have two independent “choice‐pairs”:
  – {x0a , x0b} are mutually exclusive via (2) and (4).  
  – {x1a , x1b} are mutually exclusive via (3) and (7).  

Thus there are 2×2=4 candidate sets for {x0?, x1?}.  We then close each under the remaining rules and check minimality.

1) Candidate S₁ = {x0a, x1a}.  
   – (4) applies (not x0b) ⇒ x0a (already in).  
   – (7) applies (not x1b) ⇒ x1a.  
   – From x0a or x1a, rules (1) and (5) derive qcore, then (6) derives q.  
   ⇒ S₁⁺ = {x0a, x1a, qcore, q}.  This is an answer set.

2) Candidate S₂ = {x0a, x1b}.  
   – (4) ⇒ x0a.  
   – (3) ⇒ x1b.  
   – Again x0a ⇒ qcore ⇒ q.  
   ⇒ S₂⁺ = {x0a, x1b, qcore, q}.  Also an answer set.

3) Candidate S₃ = {x0b, x1a}.  
   – (2) ⇒ x0b.  
   – (7) ⇒ x1a.  
   – x1a ⇒ qcore ⇒ q.  
   ⇒ S₃⁺ = {x0b, x1a, qcore, q}.  Also an answer set.

4) Candidate S₄ = {x0b, x1b}.  
   – (2) ⇒ x0b.  
   – (3) ⇒ x1b.  
   – Neither x0a nor x1a holds, so qcore and q do not fire.  
   ⇒ S₄⁺ = {x0b, x1b}.  Also an answer set.

We have four answer sets, three of which contain q, one of which does not. Under credulous (brave) reasoning q is true in at least one answer set, so we conclude:

ANSWER: A

Let’s identify the stable models under the Gelfond–Lifschitz reduct.  The atoms are {x1a,x1b,x0a,x0b,qcore,q}.  The rules split into two independent “exclusive‐or” pairs:

  (1) x1a ← not x1b.  
  (2) x1b ← not x1a.  

  (3) x0a ← not x0b.  
  (4) x0b ← not x0a.  

Plus the positive rules

  (5) qcore ← x1a.  
  (6) qcore ← x0a.  
  (7) q ← qcore.

The “xor” pairs (1–2) and (3–4) each force exactly one of {x1a,x1b} and one of {x0a,x0b} to be in a model.  Checking all four combinations gives exactly four stable models:

  S1 = { x1a, x0a, qcore, q }  
  S2 = { x1a, x0b, qcore, q }  
  S3 = { x1b, x0a, qcore, q }  
  S4 = { x1b, x0b }  

In S4 neither x1a nor x0a holds, so qcore and hence q do not.  Thus q is false in S4.  Since there is an answer set in which q fails, q is not true in every answer set.  

ANSWER: B

Let’s name the atoms and rules:

1.   qcore ← x1a.  
2.   x0b   ← not x0a.  
3.   x1b   ← not x1a.  
4.   x0a   ← not x0b.  
5.   qcore ← x0a.  
6.   q     ← qcore.  
7.   x1a   ← not x1b.  

We have two independent negative‐dependency loops:

•  x0a ← not x0b  
   x0b ← not x0a  

•  x1a ← not x1b  
   x1b ← not x1a  

Under well‐founded semantics every atom in a negative cycle with no external positive support becomes undefined.  Thus:

  x0a, x0b are undefined  
  x1a, x1b are undefined  

Next, qcore has only positive bodies (x1a or x0a).  Both are undefined, so neither rule can fire to make qcore true, but there is also no rule whose body is definitely false, so qcore cannot be proved false outright.  It therefore remains undefined.  

Finally q ← qcore inherits qcore’s undefined status.  

Since q is neither founded true nor founded false, its well‐founded truth value is undefined.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s name the rules in Prolog‐style for clarity:

1.  t0    :- t1.  
2.  x1a   :- not x1b.  
3.  q     :- t0.  
4.  x0b   :- not x0a.  
5.  x0a   :- not x0b.  
6.  x1b   :- not x1a.  
7.  qcore :- x1a.  
8.  t1    :- qcore.  
9.  qcore :- x0a.  

We have two independent “negation‐cycles”:

•  x0a ⇔ not x0b  
•  x1a ⇔ not x1b  

Each forces exactly one of {x0a,x0b} true and exactly one of {x1a,x1b} true in any stable (or two‐valued) model, but it does not fix *which* one.  Meanwhile

   qcore  is true if either x0a or x1a is true,  
   t1      is true if qcore,  
   t0      is true if t1,  
   q       is true if t0.  

Thus:

– If we pick x0a or x1a to be true, we get qcore→t1→t0→q, so q ends up true.  
– But we could equally well pick x0b and x1b both true (so x0a and x1a false), in which case qcore never fires and q stays false.

Since there exist consistent assignments (models) with q true and others with q false, q is not forced either way.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s attempt to prove q by Prolog‐style (negation‐as‐failure) reasoning:

1. To prove q we need t0  (rule 3).  
2. To prove t0 we need t1  (rule 1).  
3. To prove t1 we need qcore  (rule 8).  

   qcore has two clauses:
   (a) qcore ← x1a  (rule 7)  
   (b) qcore ← x0a  (rule 9)  

4. Try (a): to prove x1a we need ¬ x1b  (rule 2).  
   But x1b is defined by x1b ← ¬ x1a  (rule 6).  
   So to decide ¬ x1b we must try x1b, which in turn tries ¬ x1a, which loops back to trying x1a…  
   This never finitely succeeds or fails (infinite loop).

5. Try (b): to prove x0a we need ¬ x0b  (rule 5).  
   But x0b ← ¬ x0a  (rule 4) again yields the same kind of loop between x0a and x0b.

Neither branch for qcore finitely succeeds or finitely fails; they both loop. Hence t1, t0 and finally q also neither succeed nor finitely fail. By the given criterion (“if … does not terminate … answer ‘Cannot be determined.’”), we must conclude:

ANSWER: C

Let P be the given program.  We first isolate the two “toggle” pairs {x0a,x0b} and {x1a,x1b}.  Each pair forces exactly one atom true:

  – From rules  
     x0b ← not x0a  
     x0a ← not x0b  
    we get either x0a or x0b.  
  – From rules  
     x1a ← not x1b  
     x1b ← not x1a  
    we get either x1a or x1b.

Hence there are 2×2=4 candidates for (x0?,x1?):
  1. (x0a,x1a)
  2. (x0a,x1b)
  3. (x0b,x1a)
  4. (x0b,x1b)

We check each:

1.  x0a,x1a  
    ⇒ qcore from both x0a and x1a  
    ⇒ t1 ← qcore, so t1  
    ⇒ t0 ← t1, so t0  
    ⇒ q ← t0, so q  
   Closing under reduct yields the stable model  
     {x0a,x1a,qcore,t1,t0,q}  

2.  x0a,x1b  
    ⇒ qcore ← x0a  
    ⇒ t1,t0,q as before  
    Stable model  
     {x0a,x1b,qcore,t1,t0,q}  

3.  x0b,x1a  
    ⇒ qcore ← x1a  
    ⇒ t1,t0,q  
    Stable model  
     {x0b,x1a,qcore,t1,t0,q}  

4.  x0b,x1b  
    ⇒ no qcore (neither x0a nor x1a)  
    ⇒ no t1,t0,q  
    Stable model  
     {x0b,x1b}

In three of the four answer sets q holds.  Since q is true in at least one (indeed in three) answer sets, under credulous (brave) reasoning we conclude:

ANSWER: A

Let’s identify all answer sets under stable/answer‐set semantics:

1. The pair of rules  
   x0a ← not x0b.  
   x0b ← not x0a.  
   yields two choices: either x0a is in the answer set (and x0b is out), or vice versa.

2. Likewise  
   x1a ← not x1b.  
   x1b ← not x1a.  
   yields two choices: either x1a is in (and x1b is out) or vice versa.

So there are 4 candidate answer sets, corresponding to the four combinations of {x0a or x0b} × {x1a or x1b}.  Now qcore is derived by either of the rules

  qcore ← x1a.
